title: The grieving mothers
hookLine: women who lost children, taught by Patacara: you don't know where he came from or went (Therigatha, the five hundred)

lines: A TEACHER WHO LOST HER OWN.
cards: No one in the poem is named except the teacher. The Therigatha gives these verses to a great crowd of women, and what they share is the worst thing: each of them has lost a child. They come to Patacara.

The stories told about her say she lost her own children too, so whatever she says, she says from inside it. She doesn't offer the usual words. She doesn't say time heals, or that they'll feel better soon.
She asks a question about a road.

teach.b: Patacara says, in substance: you don't know the road he came by, or the road he left by. You don't know where he came from, or where he went. And still you cry out, my son.
Second, the turn. If you knew his road, she says, where he came from and where he went, you would not grieve like this. This is how it is for living beings.
Third, the picture. He came without being asked, and he left without asking leave.

teach.h: A TRAVELER WHO STAYED A FEW DAYS.
teach.b: He came from somewhere and stayed a few days. From here he went one way, and from there another. Read slowly, it's the image of a traveler who stopped at your house.
They speak as one: she has drawn out the arrow lodged in my heart, the one so hard to see. She has taken away my grief for my son. Notice what Patacara does not say.
She doesn't say the child didn't matter, or that the love was a mistake. Some readers hear the verses as hard, almost cold.

Others hear a release: a mother told that her child's life ran longer than the few days she was given to see. And the arrow matters. It's lodged in you by no choice of your own, and it can be drawn out.
The poem never blames the mothers for carrying it. A woman who had carried it herself is the one who pulls it free.

how: Theravada teachers can draw on Patacara's story and verses when they speak about grief, and Theravada memorial customs include chanting and offerings made in the name of the one who has died.

o: the tears shed for a child
a mourning song for the dead

games.q: Patacara and the mothers: tap the pairs.
p: where did he come from, where did he go?

s: Patacara tells the mothers that loving the child was the mistake
she says nothing like that. she asks where the child came from and where he went.
the mothers say an arrow was drawn out of their hearts
in the poem they say she pulled out the hidden arrow of grief for a son.
Patacara tells them time will heal it
she offers no such promise. she asks about the road the child came by and left by.

games.q: you're one of the mothers. Patacara has just asked where your son came from, and where he went. what do you say?
o: she can't know what this is like.
she has drawn out the arrow lodged in my heart.
games.why: in the poem the mothers answer as one: she has drawn out the hidden arrow lodged in the heart, and taken away grief for a son.

practice: This one asks for gentleness, with others and with yourself. If you are a parent who has lost a child, simply sit with your child's name and let the breath come and go at its own pace; nothing more is asked.
If you know such a parent, hold them in attention, their face, the way they say the name, without fixing anything, the way Patacara stood with the mothers who came to her.

wordCard.voice: Salla. The hidden arrow of grief that Patacara drew from the hearts of mothers who had lost a child. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali salla: an arrow or dart. The mothers say Patacara drew the hidden arrow of grief from their hearts.

carryVoice: Your line: where he came from. A traveler who stopped at the house for a few days. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

sources.ref: Therigatha 6.1 (Pancasatamatta, Patacara's five hundred: her verses to the grieving mothers and their reply)
